help.intro: A term is one entry of the shared vocabulary — a tag, an attribute label, an attribute value or a piece of text. The term itself holds no words: it is an id that other records point at, with the wording kept once per language, so renaming it changes it everywhere at once.
help.step_1_body: Type says what the term is for, not what it says: a tag labels content, an attribute label names a property ("Colour"), an attribute value fills one in ("red"), and text is free wording. It is also half of the duplicate rule, so the same word may exist once as a tag and once as an attribute value.
help.step_2_title: Write the wording, one language at a time
help.step_2_body: Each language tab holds one value, and at least one language must be filled in before the term can be saved. A tab you leave empty is simply not sent — it neither fails validation nor clears a wording already stored, because saving upserts the languages it carries and leaves the rest alone.
help.step_3_title: Expect the wording to be lower-cased
help.step_3_body: Every value is trimmed and stored in lower case, deliberately. A term is a label reused across many records, and "Summer" and "summer" rendering as two separate tags is exactly what this avoids — the stored value is the single answer to what the term says, and the display side decides how to capitalise it.
help.step_4_body: Two terms of the same type may not carry the same wording in the same language, and the check ignores case. A collision is refused with a conflict rather than merged, so the second one has to be reworded — or the existing term reused, which is usually what was meant.
help.step_5_title: Find it again, and spot the gaps
help.step_5_body: The list shows one wording per row, in the language you filter by, and keeps a term that has none in that language — an empty value is how a missing translation announces itself. Search is not limited that way: it matches the wording in any language from three characters, so a term found by its English name may still show blank under Romanian. An all-digit term is treated as an id, and the list can only be ordered by id.
help.note: Deleting a term is a soft delete and nothing checks what points at it, so records already using it keep resolving. The duplicate rule ignores deleted rows, which frees the wording immediately — and means a restore fails once another term of that type has taken it.
